14	# Cue Maximal Jump Height, Not Knee Angle; When the Dip Must Be Standard, Set It With Plinths Instead of Instructions
15	
16	**What it is** — Two notes in the starting-acceleration program (PDF 583 / p.572, checked against the page image):
17	- Vertical jumps with the bar on the shoulders: "In this exercise, as in the depth jump, the athlete must be motivated to attain the maximum jump height without thinking about the knee angle at the end of 'yielding' (pliometric) phase." Footnote 26 adds the execution: bar on the back of the shoulders, feet "about hip-width apart", "Quickly squat down and jump straight up as high as you can. Stop and shake your legs (you can rack the bar if desired)", and "the previous pliometric phase must be executed in the way that assures the consecutive best jump height automatically, thanks to the athlete's correct understanding of the motor concepts involved in this exercise."
18	- Kettlebell squat jumps, footnote 27: consecutive vertical jumps "standing on two high parallel benches or plinths. During execution of this exercise, the kettlebell must come close to the floor in the low down position, but should not touch the floor. In this way, one can ensure a standard leg flexion angle, determined by the height of the plinths." Fig 22 shows three frames: standing on two stands with the bell between the feet, squatting with the bell near the floor between the stands, and jumping up (an up-down arrow beside the figure).
19	
20	**Why it works** — His stated reason for the first: the yielding phase should organise itself "automatically" around the goal of best height, through "correct understanding of the motor concepts" (footnote 26). For the second, his stated reason is that the plinths "ensure a standard leg flexion angle" (footnote 27). Inference: the set-up means the athlete need not think about depth, and both remove joint-angle attention from the athlete during the jump; one leaves depth to the goal, the other builds it into the set-up.
21	
22	**When to apply** — When coaching loaded or depth jumps, give the outcome (jump as high as possible, reach a marker) rather than a knee-angle instruction. When a fixed squat depth matters (for comparing sets, or for a weaker athlete who would sink too deep), use a physical stop such as plinths or a box under the bell. This matches the 9.2 depth-jump technique note to reach "some height, indicated by a marker" (PDF 576 / p.565; see [[heuristic--depth-jump-execution-cues-landing-gaze-breath]]).
23	
24	**When NOT to apply** — He gives no study; the cue is a coaching opinion. It does not override the leg program's squat-jump instruction that thighs go "at least parallel to the floor" (PDF 578 / p.567), which is a depth instruction for a different exercise. Inference: an athlete who lands with knees collapsing inward still needs a technique correction; "don't think about the knee angle" is about depth at the end of the dip, not about knee alignment. The plinth set-up adds a fall risk with a loaded bell, which he does not discuss.
25	
26	**Example** — His Fig 22: kettlebell squat jumps between two plinths, the bell stopping just short of the floor each rep so every rep reaches the same knee flexion (PDF 583 / p.572).
27

14	# Verkhoshansky's 6-Week Ball-Throwing Speed Program: Heavy (80%) Then Light (40%) Throws Against a Cable Apparatus, Sized From Maximal Effort in the Start Position
15	
16	**What it is** — "Program for improvement of ball throwing speed" (PDF 586-588 / pp.575-577, read from the page images). It combines "light and heavy weight throwing using a special training apparatus" (Fig 23, two drawings: an athlete beside a tall vertical guide carrying a weight, and an athlete in the throwing position holding a ball attached by a horizontal cable to a gridded frame; the drawings do not show how the parts connect). Load setting: "measure the maximum effort that can be displayed by the player in the starting position for the ball throw. The light weight is equal 40% and the heavy one, 80% of this value. For example, if the maximum effort is 20 kg, the training weights will be equal to 8 kg and 18 kg respectively" (PDF 586 / p.575). Method: "the repeat-serial method. One series includes the heavy and the light weight with the first exercise executed with the heavy weight"; "a series of 1x4 with heavy weight and then 2x7 with light weight" is one set of 4 heavy then 2 sets of 7 light; 1-2 min between sets, series repeated "several times" with 4-6 min between; when maximal effort rises, "the training weights should be increased accordingly" (PDF 586). The schedule (PDF 587-588 / pp.576-577) runs five days a week for weeks 1-5 and four days in week 6. Heavy sets rise from 1 x 4 to 1 x 6; light work ranges from 1 x 8 to 4 x 8; series per session rise from 2 (weeks 1-3) to 3 (week 4) and 4 (week 5, days 1-2), then return to 2 (week 5 days 3-5, week 6), with several days mixing two series formats.
17	
18	**Recorded as printed:** 80% of 20 kg is 16 kg, not the printed 18 kg (Inference: arithmetic or typographic error; 40% of 20 kg = 8 kg is right). Week 1 day 5 prints "1 x 4 with heavy weight and 2x3 with light weight" (PDF 587 / p.576), out of line with the 2 x 7 to 4 x 8 light sets around it (Inference: possible misprint for 2 x 8).
19	
20	**Why it works** — He gives no mechanism on these pages beyond the heavy-first order. Inference: it is a heavy-light contrast series of the kind the authors classify among contrast methods in 7.1 ([[framework--contrast-methods-load-release-pneumatics-heavy-light-set]]), and loads set from effort in the throwing start position keep the resistance specific to that joint configuration. The 5.2.3 implement findings warn that too heavy an implement can harm technique ([[claim--implement-mass-for-speed-strength-keep-technique-and-size-per-athlete]]); the 80% heavy load here is a cable resistance, not a heavier ball.
21	
22	**When to apply** — An off-season block for throwing athletes (the text says "players"; the sport is not named) with access to a cable or pulley that can be set from a measured isometric effort in the throwing start position. Keep heavy first in each series, set loads from a fresh maximum, and re-test. Plan around the expected loss of throwing feel ([[heuristic--warn-throwers-the-feel-of-the-ball-fades-and-allow-2-3-weeks-to-restore]]).
23	
24	**When NOT to apply** — No outcome, population or throwing-speed data is given. The 18 kg example contradicts the 80% rule; use the rule, not the example. The apparatus is drawn, not specified (pulley ratio, handle, load path), so the 40%/80% loads cannot be copied to a different machine without re-measuring. Five days a week for six weeks with throwing technique degraded from week 3 (PDF 588 / p.577) does not fit an in-season period.
25	
26	**Example** — Week 4, day 3: 1 x 4 heavy and 2 x 8 light, the series repeated 3 times, then 1 x 4 heavy and 3 x 8 light (PDF 587 / p.576).
27

15	
16	**What it is** — "Important additional information about the program" after the ball-throwing program (PDF 588 / p.577, checked against the page image):
17	1. "It is possible that players will lose 'the feeling of the ball' (the feel of the throw) when the strength program is used (especially beginning the 3rd week). This is a natural result of the strength training. The coach must explain the cause of this phenomenon to players. He must also tell them that it is a temporary phenomenon and that the 'feeling of throwing' will come back when the program is completed."
18	2. "The low ability to throw the ball as a result of the strength training should be kept in mind when technical-tactical mastery is an aim of training."
19	3. "The weeks following the strength program play an important role in the training process. First of all, the load on the muscles of the throwing arm must be excluded during the first week. Then the power of throwing should be increased gradually. As a rule, 2-3 weeks is enough for the restoration of the feeling of throwing."
20	
21	**Why it works** — He calls the loss "a natural result of the strength training" and gives no mechanism. Inference: this is the pattern the book describes as the long-term delayed training effect, where voluminous strength loading depresses speed-strength preparedness during the block and the gain appears after it ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]); 5.3.1 also reports that heavy strength volume can reduce explosiveness and technique ([[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]]).
22

Eric's baseline: the department's game week ends "lifting and hard practice ... 72 hours before a Saturday game" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: a 2-3 week restoration window is far longer than an in-season week allows, so blocks like this belong off-season.
24	
25	**When NOT to apply** — The timings (week 3 onset, one week off, 2-3 weeks to restore) are his rule of thumb for this program, with no data, sport or athlete numbers. They should not be transferred to a different strength program without checking. "Feeling" is subjective and he gives no way to measure it. Inference: a drop in throwing feel that persists past 2-3 weeks, or comes with pain, is a reason to look for overload or injury, not a sign to wait longer.
26	
27	**Example** — His own: after the six-week heavy-light throwing program, no throwing-arm loading in week 7, then gradually rising throwing power, with feel back by about weeks 8-9 (PDF 588 / p.577; week numbers counted by this entry).

# A Throwing-Strength Block Temporarily Costs "the Feeling of the Ball": Warn the Players, Keep Technical Goals Out of It, Then Rest the Arm a Week and Allow 2-3 Weeks

**What it is** — "Important additional information about the program" after the ball-throwing program (PDF 588 / p.577, checked against the page image):
1. "It is possible that players will lose 'the feeling of the ball' (the feel of the throw) when the strength program is used (especially beginning the 3rd week). This is a natural result of the strength training. The coach must explain the cause of this phenomenon to players. He must also tell them that it is a temporary phenomenon and that the 'feeling of throwing' will come back when the program is completed."
2. "The low ability to throw the ball as a result of the strength training should be kept in mind when technical-tactical mastery is an aim of training."
3. "The weeks following the strength program play an important role in the training process. First of all, the load on the muscles of the throwing arm must be excluded during the first week. Then the power of throwing should be increased gradually. As a rule, 2-3 weeks is enough for the restoration of the feeling of throwing."

**Why it works** — He calls the loss "a natural result of the strength training" and gives no mechanism. Inference: this is the pattern the book describes as the long-term delayed training effect, where voluminous strength loading depresses speed-strength preparedness during the block and the gain appears after it ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]); 5.3.1 also reports that heavy strength volume can reduce explosiveness and technique ([[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]]).

**When to apply** — Before any concentrated strength or contrast block for throwers or other skill-speed athletes: tell athletes and sport coaches in advance that feel may drop from about week 3 and why; do not schedule technical-tactical goals that depend on throwing feel inside the block; after it, a week with no throwing-arm load, then a gradual build over 2-3 weeks. Eric's baseline: the department's game week ends "lifting and hard practice ... 72 hours before a Saturday game" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: a 2-3 week restoration window is far longer than an in-season week allows, so blocks like this belong off-season.

**When NOT to apply** — The timings (week 3 onset, one week off, 2-3 weeks to restore) are his rule of thumb for this program, with no data, sport or athlete numbers. They should not be transferred to a different strength program without checking. "Feeling" is subjective and he gives no way to measure it. Inference: a drop in throwing feel that persists past 2-3 weeks, or comes with pain, is a reason to look for overload or injury, not a sign to wait longer.

**Example** — His own: after the six-week heavy-light throwing program, no throwing-arm loading in week 7, then gradually rising throwing power, with feel back by about weeks 8-9 (PDF 588 / p.577; week numbers counted by this entry).

# Verkhoshansky: The Shock Method Is a Forced Shock Stretch of Tensed Muscle, a Different Entity From "Plyometrics", and He Is Not Its "Father"

**What it is** — Section 9.2 is a first-person paper by Verkhoshansky ("Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky" under the heading, PDF 574 / p.563). He defines the method: "The regime, in which an external resistance is actively overcome after being preceded by a sharp preliminary stretch of the muscles, is most effective for training explosive strength (Verkhoshansky, 1960). This technique is called the Shock Method for development of explosive strength and reactive ability (Verkhoshansky, 1961)." He then says: "in USA the Shock Method is most often called *plyometrics*. This is not correct. The Shock Method and plyometric training are different entities" (PDF 574 / p.563). Under "I am not the father of plyometrics" he says being called "father of plyometrics" "gives me pleasure to hear this, but it is incorrect"; the term "to name my shock method, was invented by my friend, Fred Wilt", a former Olympic runner, NCAA champion and Purdue track coach, with whom he "corresponded ... in the 1960's" (PDF 575 / p.564). He warns that "plyometrics" "could be confused with the term 'pliometric'", the old anatomy term for the "yielding" regime in which "the external load on the muscles is much greater than the tension developed during the contraction, when the muscles are stretching" (footnote 23 cites Faulkner, 2003, J Appl Physiol 95: 455-459, and Faulkner et al., 1997, MSSE 29(5)). His defining feature: "The specific characteristic of my method is expressed in **the shock stretch of the muscle under tension**. This method has a compulsory (forced) character when the neuromuscular system is forced to display a high level of power against a significant external mechanical influence" (PDF 575 / p.564, bold on the page; all quotes checked against the page images).

**Why it works** — His stated reasoning: the shock stretch of strained muscle is "a high powered training influence for the neuromuscular system" because the system is forced, by an external mechanical impact, to produce high power (PDF 575 / p.564). The forcing comes from outside (the fall), not from the athlete's intent. Inference: this is why he separates it from "plyometric training": a jump the athlete starts voluntarily, with no imposed impact, lacks the "compulsory" element he names as the method's specific characteristic. He does not spell out which drills fall on which side.

**When to apply** — When a programme lists "plyometrics", use his test: is there an external impact that sharply stretches muscle already under tension (a depth jump, a drop catch), or only a self-started jump? Only the first is his shock method. This sharpens the 1.6 terminology entry ([[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]), which reports the authors' wider point that Western "plyometrics" drifted to cover ordinary jumping. Eric's baseline: "we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 76, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)). Inference: when DSI points to "more plyometric training", his distinction asks whether that means shock-method depth jumps or submaximal jumping, which carry different loads.

**When NOT to apply** — The history is his own account, with no source beyond the footnotes on Wilt's books (footnote 22, a bookfinder URL) and the Faulkner terminology papers. The publisher's back cover (PDF 590, not part of 9.2) calls him "the Russian researcher who invented plyometric training"; that is the publisher's wording, which his own text rejects. "Different entities" is asserted, not defined drill by drill, so do not use it to rule a specific drill in or out without the impact test above (Inference). The 1960 and 1961 dates are his self-citations; the 9.2 paper gives no bibliography for them.

**Example** — His own: the depth jump, where landing from a height imposes "a sharp preliminary stretch" on tensed leg extensors before the take-off (PDF 574-575 / pp.563-564).

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (1.6, the pliometric, miometric, isometric scheme and the authors' precise definition); [[case-study--half-squat-back-pain-and-triple-jump-takeoff-led-verkhoshansky-to-depth-jumps]] (the origin story in the same paper); [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (reactive ability); [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[principle--reserve-the-shock-method-for-experienced-top-level-athletes-not-youth]]

**Why it works** — His stated reasoning: the shock stretch of strained muscle is "a high powered training influence for the neuromuscular system" because the system is forced, by an external mechanical impact, to produce high power (PDF 575 / p.564). Inference: the forcing comes from outside (the fall), not from the athlete's intent; this is why he separates it from "plyometric training": a jump the athlete starts voluntarily, with no imposed impact, lacks the "compulsory" element he names as the method's specific characteristic. He does not spell out which drills fall on which side.

**When to apply** — When a programme lists "plyometrics", Inference: a test drawn from his definition: is there an external impact that sharply stretches muscle already under tension (a depth jump, a drop catch), or only a self-started jump? On that reading, only the first is his shock method. This sharpens the 1.6 terminology entry ([[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]), which reports the authors' wider point that Western "plyometrics" drifted to cover ordinary jumping. Eric's baseline: "we incorporate the countermovement jump and the isometric mid-thigh pull to get a dynamic strength index, to determine whether we need more plyometric training or more max-strength training" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 76, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q21)). Inference: when DSI points to "more plyometric training", his distinction asks whether that means shock-method depth jumps or submaximal jumping, which carry different loads.

**When NOT to apply** — The history is his own account, with no source beyond the footnotes on Wilt's books (footnote 22, a bookfinder URL) and the Faulkner terminology papers. The publisher's back cover (PDF 590, not part of 9.2) calls him "the Russian researcher who invented plyometric training"; that is the publisher's wording, which his own text rejects. "Different entities" is asserted, not defined drill by drill, so do not use it to rule a specific drill in or out without the impact test above (Inference). The 1960 and 1961 dates are his self-citations; the 9.2 paper gives no bibliography for them.

**Example** — His own: the depth jump, where landing from a height imposes "a sharp preliminary stretch" on tensed leg extensors before the take-off (PDF 574-575 / pp.563-564).

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (1.6, the pliometric, miometric, isometric scheme and the authors' precise definition); [[case-study--half-squat-back-pain-and-triple-jump-takeoff-led-verkhoshansky-to-depth-jumps]] (the origin story in the same paper); [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (reactive ability); [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[principle--reserve-the-shock-method-for-experienced-top-level-athletes-not-youth]]; [[claim--popular-plyometric-drills-work-through-other-mechanisms]] (5.2.4, PDF 293-294 / pp.282-283: most drills called "plyometric" are not the shock mechanism, sorted drill by drill, which 9.2 does not do)

# Most "Plyometric" Drills in Popular Western Books Work Through Eccentric Loading, Connective Tissue, Starting Strength and Prestretch, Not the Shock Mechanism

**What it is** — Under "Popular Information on Plyometrics" (PDF pp. 293-294 / printed pp. 282-283; p. 293 verified against the page image, p. 294 from the text layer):
- Popular Western texts ("e.g. Chu, 1992; Radcliffe & Farantinos, 1985") present jumping and rebound activities "many of which do not constitute true plyometric training as originally conceived by Russian scientists"; they are "often supplementary or preparatory movements."
- "Most books classify extended range swinging, passing or catching of medicine balls or other objects as 'plyometric', although the amortisation phase is too long to produce classical plyometrics." These drills still help "eye-hand coordination, eccentric strength and starting strength, but they are not strictly plyometric."
- Books omit the tonic versus phasic myotatic reflex in relation to drill types, the positive supportive reaction, the crossed extensor reflex, phased breathing, the maximal-submaximal distinction, and concurrent and sequential prescription.
- "the so-called plyometric drills in current Western texts are known to enhance performance, but it is not predominantly due to plyometric training, but more to the increased loading of eccentric contraction, the conditioning of connective tissue, the improvement of voluntary starting strength from the quasi-isometric state, the use of prestretch, and enhancement of acceleration strength by increasing the velocity of projectiles such as medicine balls" (PDF p. 294 / printed p. 283).
- The physiotherapy link: in PNF a therapist "sometimes imposes a short, sharp jerk on an eccentrically or isometrically contracting muscle to produce strong muscle contraction in a weakened muscle", principles that "preceded sporting plyometrics by several decades" (same page).
- Related, from the classification passage: *pseudo-plyometrics* such as aerobics "power moves" and many "water plyos" lack "an explosive rebound phase with a short coupling time" (PDF p. 284 / printed p. 273, verified against the page image).

**Why it works** — The text's argument is definitional: long amortisation phases fall outside the shock method, so the benefit must come from the other listed qualities. It gives no study separating these mechanisms.

**When to apply** — Labelling a program's med-ball and jump drills honestly: Inference: a long-amortisation med-ball chest pass or rotational throw is a starting-strength and eccentric drill in the authors' terms, and should not be counted as shock-method volume or dosed with shock-method rest.

**When NOT to apply** — `untested`: the list of "other mechanisms" is the text's assertion, with no data. The criticism of specific books is the author's opinion and was not checked against those books. Not a reason to drop these drills: the text says they "are known to enhance performance."

**Example** — The text's own: extended-range medicine ball swinging and catching, called plyometric in popular books, as an example of a drill whose amortisation is too long for classical plyometrics (PDF p. 293 / printed p. 282).

**Related** — [[framework--plyometric-training-classification-impact-intensity-and-function]]; [[heuristic--plyometric-training-coupling-under-0-15-s-feedforward-and-force-time-pattern]]; [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]; [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]]

# Verkhoshansky's 12-Week Leg Program: Heavy Squats, Then Loaded Jumps and Interval Squats, Then Depth Jumps, Then Box Jumps

**What it is** — "Program to develop explosive strength and reactive ability of the leg muscles" (PDF 578-582 / pp.567-571; every number below was read from the page images, since the table OCR is unreliable). Twelve weeks, two sessions a week for weeks 1-8, then "From the 9th week on, from day 17 - 28, workouts are executed three times a week" (the table numbers these as sessions 17-28). Four means: depth jump; barbell squat; consecutive barbell jumps, either squat jumps with the bar on the shoulders ("thighs are at least parallel to the floor", underlined on the page) or barbell scissor-lunge jumps (Fig 19); and box jumps, "Consecutive jumps onto a box and down using a double leg takeoff", box "0.4 - 0.8 m" (Fig 20). Loads are % of squat 1RM; "8 x 10 (2)" means 2 series of 8 sets of 10 (PDF 578 / p.567). The phases:

| Weeks (sessions) | Content |
|---|---|
| 1-3 (1-6) | Squats only. Heavy days pair 90% or 93-95% (2-4 x 3-5 or 3-5 x 2-3, rest 4-6 min) with 80-85% volume sets (2-3 x 10-12 to 3-5 x 8-10); pyramid days (80% 1 x 10, 90% 1 x 5, 90-95% 1 x 2; or 70% 1 x 12, 80% 1 x 10, 85% 1 x 7) repeated 2-3 times |
| 4-5 (7-10) | Consecutive barbell jumps at 40%, 5 x 8 (2) then 8 x 8 (2), 60 s between sets; squats at 85-90% then 95% "using the interval method", 4-5 x 1-3 |
| 6-8 (11-16) | Depth jumps, 3-4 sets of 10 per session in total, mostly split between 0.75 m and 1.10 m (session 14: 4 x 10 from 0.75 m only), then 6-12 min rest, then barbell jumps at 40%, 6-10 sets of 8-10, set rest falling from 60 s to 30 s to 10 s |
| 9-11 (17-25) | Three sessions a week: two depth-jump days (4 x 10 from 1.10 m or 0.75 m, then barbell jumps 8-10 x 10 in 2-4 series) and one box-jump day (0.4-0.5 m 4 x 40 (2); 0.5-0.6 m 6 x 40 (2); 0.7-0.8 m 5 x 50 (3)) |
| 12 (26-28) | Barbell jumps 10 x 10 (3-4), 10 s between sets, twice; box jumps 0.7-0.8 m 6 x 50 (3), 2 min between sets |

Footnote 24: after the last 85% squat rep "it is necessary to do 2-3 additional repetitions" (PDF 579 / p.568). Footnote 25 defines the interval method (see [[framework--interval-resistance-training-and-cluster-sets]], Also in 9.2). The rules that follow the table are in [[heuristic--keep-the-order-of-means-and-reset-jump-load-to-40-percent-of-current-squat-max]].

**Recorded as printed (Inference: likely misprints):** sessions 12 and 13 list "Depth Jumps (0.10 m.)" as the second height, where every other session pairs 0.75 m with 1.10 m (PDF 580 / p.569); session 11 prints "8 x 10 (6)", six series, where every other barbell-jump row has 2 to 4 (PDF 580); the text says "day 17 - 28" for what the table calls training sessions (PDF 578).

**Why it works** — His stated principle, printed after the table: "gradually increasing the specificity and intensity of the training load", so "each training load prepares the organism for effective execution the following loads" (PDF 582 / p.571). Inference: the order (maximal strength first, then light loaded jumps, then depth jumps, then high-contact box jumps) matches the strength-first sequences reported in 5.3 and 6.9.1 ([[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[case-study--barbell-and-depth-jump-sequences-in-high-jumpers]]). The drop heights match the 0.75-1.15 m range of 4.2.3 ([[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]), with 1.10 m, not 1.15 m, as the high one.

**When to apply** — As a template for an off-season reactive block for jumpers or other leg-dominant power athletes who already squat heavily, keeping the phase order and the 40% barbell-jump load. Eric's baseline: "Prilepin's chart (total reps and reps-per-set by %1RM) is the default guide for daily rep/set assignment within a training block" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 107, Inferred/Explicit (shared team material)). Inference: the weeks 1-3 squat rows (for example 3-5 x 2-3 at 93-95%, 2 x 8 + 2-3 at 85%) can be checked against that chart before use.

**When NOT to apply** — No outcome data, population or sport is given for the program; it is a prescription. The contact counts are large: 10 x 10 barbell jumps in 3-4 series is 300-400 loaded jumps in a session, and 6 x 50 box jumps in 3 series is 900 contacts, which, Inference, sits awkwardly beside his own rule that "It is the quality of the shock method, not the quantity that is important" (PDF 577 / p.566, item 7). Inference: the barbell and box jumps are submaximal rebound work, not shock-method depth jumps, which stay at 4 x 10 or less per session, within his item 2 cap (PDF 577). His conclusions restrict the shock method to "experienced top level athletes" (PDF 588 / p.577), so this is not a youth or novice program ([[principle--reserve-the-shock-method-for-experienced-top-level-athletes-not-youth]]). In-season football weeks do not fit a three-session-a-week reactive block (Inference).

**Example** — Session 16 (week 8): depth jumps 0.75 m 2 x 10 and 1.10 m 2 x 10, 6-8 min rest, then barbell jumps at 40% 8 x 10 in 2-3 series, 30 s between sets and 8-12 min between series (PDF 581 / p.570).

**Related** — [[heuristic--keep-the-order-of-means-and-reset-jump-load-to-40-percent-of-current-squat-max]]; [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]; [[heuristic--maximal-plyometric-and-depth-jump-volume-and-rest]]; [[claim--depth-jump-training-beat-higher-volume-traditional-training-in-jumpers]] (5.2.4, 475 depth jumps in 12 weeks); [[framework--interval-resistance-training-and-cluster-sets]]; [[case-study--six-week-starting-acceleration-program-squats-loaded-jumps-depth-jumps-bounds-hills]]

# Verkhoshansky's 6-Week Starting-Acceleration Program: Squats, Loaded and Kettlebell Jumps, Depth Jumps, Multiple Bounds, Stadium Jumps and Short Hills

**What it is** — "Program for Perfecting Starting Acceleration" (PDF 583-586 / pp.572-575; numbers read from the page images, since the table OCR scrambles the rows). It "is executed two times a week for six weeks for a total of 12 training sessions" with seven means (PDF 583-584):
1. Barbell squats at "80-90% of maximum for development of maximum strength and for toning the central nervous system".
2. Vertical jumps with the bar on the shoulders (Fig 21) "using a weight of 30-50% of maximum", for explosive strength.
3. Kettlebell squat jumps (Fig 22), 16, 24 or 32 kg "chosen depending upon the athlete", for reactive ability; a dumbbell will do if no kettlebell is available.
4. Depth jumps, for explosive strength and reactive ability.
5. Six-fold and ten-fold "leg-to-leg bounds from place executed with maximum effort", for "repeated explosive effort and anaerobic capacity".
6. Stadium jumps up stairs, "for development of maximal anaerobic capacity", "2-3 steps at a time with an active take-off in an upward and forward direction".
7. Uphill running, 15-25 m, "at a low rate with emphasis on a forward take-off and active swing movements of the leg. Running with half bent legs like dribbling is a huge mistake: it lowers the specificity of the training influence of this exercise."

The sessions: 1, 2 and 4 are squats only (85-90% 2-3 x 5-6; then pyramids); 3 and 7 pair bar jumps with six-fold bounds; 5 pairs depth jumps (0.75 m, 2 x 10) with ten-fold bounds; 6 pairs kettlebell squat jumps 3 x 8 with ten-fold bounds; 7, 9 and 11 end with uphill runs 1 x 5-6 after 15 min rest; 8, 10 and 12 are depth jumps 4 x 10 (0.75 m in session 8, 1.10 m in 10 and 12) then stadium jumps 4 x 10 in 2-3 series; 9 and 11 pair squats at 93-95% 2 x 2-3 with depth jumps from 1.10 m, 2 x 10 (PDF 584-586 / pp.573-575). Rests are long: 4-6 min between sets and 8-12 min between series.

**Recorded as printed (Inference: likely errors):** the exercise list gives the bar jumps at "30-50% of maximum" (PDF 583), but sessions 3 and 7 prescribe "Vertical jumps with bar (50-60%)" (PDF 584-585). Session 2 gives "(93-95%)" for "1 x 12" (PDF 584 / p.573), while the same pyramid in the leg program puts 1 x 2 at the top load (PDF 579 / p.568). The book does not reconcile either.

**Why it works** — His stated purposes are per means (list above): maximal strength and CNS "toning" from squats, explosive strength from loaded jumps, reactive ability from kettlebell and depth jumps, repeated explosive effort and anaerobic capacity from bounds and stairs, and a specific forward take-off from hills. Inference: the program moves from mostly squats (sessions 1-4) toward depth jumps, stairs and hills (sessions 8-12), the same rising specificity as the leg program.

**When to apply** — A short pre-season block for athletes whose event starts from rest (sprint starts, football get-off), who already squat and jump. The hill cue is concrete: forward take-off and active leg swing, not a shuffling, bent-leg run. Eric's baseline: "0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development)" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 94, Legacy (interview 2026-09-28, Q8)). Inference: that reading matches his mix of heavy squats and loaded jumps for starting acceleration; a 0-10 m split before and after the six weeks would test it.

**When NOT to apply** — No outcome data, sport, level or test is given. Stadium jumps and bounds are aimed at "anaerobic capacity", which is not a starting-acceleration quality; Inference: they serve repeat-effort ability, and could be cut for an athlete who only needs single starts. Depth jumps from 1.10 m in four sessions limit this to athletes who meet his "experienced top level" condition ([[principle--reserve-the-shock-method-for-experienced-top-level-athletes-not-youth]]). Do not quote the bar-jump load without the 30-50% and 50-60% conflict.

**Example** — Session 9: squats at 93-95% 2 x 2-3 paired with depth jumps from 1.10 m 2 x 10, the pair repeated twice with 10-12 min between series; then 15 min rest and 5-6 uphill runs of 15-25 m with 4-6 min between (PDF 585 / p.574).

**Related** — [[heuristic--cue-maximal-jump-height-not-knee-angle-and-fix-depth-with-plinths]] (footnotes 26-27 on the two loaded jumps); [[case-study--twelve-week-leg-program-squats-then-barbell-jumps-then-depth-and-box-jumps]]; [[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]]; [[claim--optimal-depth-jump-drop-height-for-power-vs-force]]; [[heuristic--cyclic-vs-acyclic-speed-strength-tempo-rest-and-fatigue]]

# Verkhoshansky's 6-Week Starting-Acceleration Program: Squats, Loaded and Kettlebell Jumps, Depth Jumps, Multiple Bounds, Stadium Jumps and Short Hills

**What it is** — "Program for Perfecting Starting Acceleration" (PDF 583-586 / pp.572-575; numbers read from the page images, since the table OCR scrambles the rows). It "is executed two times a week for six weeks for a total of 12 training sessions" with seven means (PDF 583-584):
1. Barbell squats at "80-90% of maximum for development of maximum strength and for toning the central nervous system".
2. Vertical jumps with the bar on the shoulders (Fig 21) "using a weight of 30-50% of maximum", for explosive strength.
3. Kettlebell squat jumps (Fig 22), 16, 24 or 32 kg "chosen depending upon the athlete", for reactive ability; a dumbbell will do if no kettlebell is available.
4. Depth jumps, for explosive strength and reactive ability.
5. Six-fold and ten-fold "leg-to-leg bounds from place executed with maximum effort", for "repeated explosive effort and anaerobic capacity".
6. Stadium jumps up stairs, "for development of maximal anaerobic capacity", "2-3 steps at a time with an active take-off in an upward and forward direction".
7. Uphill running, 15-25 m, "at a low rate with emphasis on a forward take-off and active swing movements of the leg. Running with half bent legs like dribbling is a huge mistake: it lowers the specificity of the training influence of this exercise."

The sessions: 1, 2 and 4 are squats only (85-90% 2-3 x 5-6; then pyramids); 3 and 7 pair bar jumps with six-fold bounds; 5 pairs depth jumps (0.75 m, 2 x 10) with ten-fold bounds; 6 pairs kettlebell squat jumps 3 x 8 with ten-fold bounds; 7, 9 and 11 end with uphill runs 1 x 5-6 after 15 min rest; 8, 10 and 12 are depth jumps 4 x 10 (0.75 m in session 8, 1.10 m in 10 and 12) then stadium jumps 4 x 10 in 2-3 series; 9 and 11 pair squats at 93-95% 2 x 2-3 with depth jumps from 1.10 m, 2 x 10 (PDF 584-586 / pp.573-575). # Junior Sprinters: Short Jumps Trained Stride, Long Jumps Trained Top Speed, and the Combination Was Called a Summation

**What it is** — "In an experiment with junior class sprinters" three groups trained "for a period of eight months": one did mainly short jumps (repeated jumps on one and two legs, triple and quintuple standing broad jumps), one mainly long jumping exercises ("multiple jumps on one leg or from leg to leg over distances of 30-100m"), and one did both (PDF pp. 299-300 / printed pp. 288-289). The authors report: "The short jumping exercises developed primarily length and speed of the running stride, whereas the long jumping exercises largely increased maximum running speed and speed-strength endurance. The combination of short and long jumping exercises led to a summation of their separate training effects and the development of speed-strength abilities which are specific to sprinters" (PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289). Fig 5.12 (verified against the page image) plots the decrease in sprint time in seconds for each group at 30 m and 60 m from a low start (LS) and a standing start (SS), and at 100 m from a low start. Approximate bar heights read from the image (short / long / combined): 30 m LS about 0.39 / 0.08 / 0.25 s; 30 m SS about 0.08 / 0.14 / 0.19 s; 60 m LS about 0.27 / 0.20 / 0.29 s; 60 m SS about 0.07 / 0.38 / 0.42 s; 100 m LS about 0.29 / 0.48 / 1.0 s (the 100 m panel uses a 0 to 1.0 s scale). An outlined bar at the right edge of the 100 m panel also reaches 1.0; it may be part of the frame and is unclear. No group sizes or statistics are given.

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism beyond the outcome labels: short jumps act on stride length and stride speed, long jumps on maximum speed and speed-strength endurance, and the two "summate." Inference: the split matches the jump durations (brief standing multi-jumps vs bounding over 30-100 m), but the text does not draw that link.

**When to apply** — Choosing jump means for sprint development: the authors' data suggest short, standing multi-jumps and long bounding series train different parts of the sprint, so a sprint-focused off-season can include both. Inference: for football, short jumps map to the start and early acceleration distances and long bounds to the longer runs, but the authors tested junior track sprinters, not football players.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book (text vs figure).** The text calls the combined effect "a summation of their separate training effects," but in Fig 5.12 the short-jump group, not the combined group, shows the largest drop at 30 m LS (about 0.39 vs 0.25 s). The combined group is largest at the other four distances. Against the sum of the two single groups, the combined bar is below it at 30 m SS (0.19 vs 0.22) and 60 m LS (0.29 vs 0.47) (and at 30 m LS, 0.25 vs 0.47), about equal at 60 m SS (0.42 vs 0.45), and above it only at 100 m LS (1.0 vs 0.77). Inference: on these readings "summation" fits only the 100 m result. The bar values above are read by eye from a printed chart and are approximate. The subjects were junior sprinters; the authors give no data for senior athletes.

**Example** — The authors' own: over 100 m from a low start, the combined jump group improved by about 1.0 s, against about 0.29 s for short jumps alone and about 0.48 s for long jumps alone (Fig 5.12, PDF p. 300 / printed p. 289).

# Alternate-Leg Bounding for Sprinters: Gather the Planted Leg Through Hip Flexion, 50-100 m, With 100-150 g Thigh Cuffs (Verkhoshansky's Practice)

**What it is** — "In certain cases, power can be increased without using additional loads. For example, with jumps from one leg to the other, the push-off displays values of power which are greater than in running. Therefore, these jumps are excellent for the special strength training of sprinters." They must be done "by not accentuating the push-off of the body (which does not happen in sprinting), but by active gathering-in of the planted leg (i.e. via hip flexion)." "These jumps should be executed repetitively over distances of 50-100 meters as fast as possible. The addition of small cuffs weighing from 100-150 grams on each thigh can makes such exercises more effective in experienced athletes (based on Verkhoshansky's experience with top Russian sprinters, such as Zubov)" (PDF p. 278 / printed p. 267, verified against the page image). The passage names Verkhoshansky in the third person, so this account is Siff's report of Verkhoshansky's coaching practice.

**Why it works** — The given reason is that bounding push-offs show more power than running push-offs, so they overload the sprint push-off without external weight. No power values, method of measurement or source are given. Inference: the cue to gather the planted leg rather than push off keeps the drill close to sprint mechanics, which matches the book's dynamic-correspondence argument, though the passage does not say so.

**When to apply** — Eric's baseline: Issurin's residual effects drive "our speed programming in the off-season and ... sprinting recommendations in season" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 97, Explicit, Q16). Inference: bounding for 50-100 m is a candidate speed-strength means for skill players in the off-season speed block, with the hip-flexion "gather" cue as the coaching point; thigh cuffs belong only to experienced athletes, as the authors say.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one coach's experience reported second-hand, with no data; the "greater power than running" claim has no figures. The cuffs are reserved for "experienced athletes." Inference: 50-100 m of maximal bounding is a high-volume plyometric dose for heavy athletes such as linemen, and the passage gives no set or rep count. Bondarchuk's correlation data support leg-to-leg jumps for sprinters, but are a separate source with its own population. Moyer also argues for gram-level limb loads in sprinting, but the library entry on that claim finds his kinetic-energy numbers do not hold, so it does not add support for the cuffs.

**Example** — The authors' own case: Verkhoshansky's top Russian sprinters, Zubov named, bounding with 100-150 g cuffs on each thigh (PDF p. 278 / printed p. 267).

**Related** — [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--sprint-jump-exercises-most-transferable-assistance]] (leg-to-leg jumps for 50 m transferred to 100 m results at all levels); [[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--wearable-resistance-kinetic-energy-sprint]]; [[heuristic--train-coupled-hip-flexion-extension-without-heavily-loaded-simulation]]; [[heuristic--cyclic-vs-acyclic-speed-strength-tempo-rest-and-fatigue]]

# Arm Throw Height After Barbell Presses: The After-Effect Experiment Behind Table 5.3 and Fig 5.4

**What it is** — "The progressive development of speed-strength is the result of combining means for exploiting the after-effect phenomenon of preceding work to increase the effectiveness of subsequent work." In an "exercise modelling" experiment, "the working effect of an explosive movement, as measured by the height to which a load was thrown (Fig 5.4), increases by an average of 38-40% after execution of barbell presses for 3 sets of 3 repetitions with 80% of the 1RM (with a rest interval of 10 minutes between the pressing and the throwing)," with shorter movement time and greater working path, average speed, driving force and power (PDF p. 276 / printed p. 265). Table 5.3, "Arm movement characteristics for throwing a weight before and after tonic work (Verkhoshansky, 1977)" (PDF p. 277 / printed p. 266, verified against the page image):

| Characteristic | First effort | Second effort | Difference (%) as printed |
|---|---|---|---|
| Height of throw (cm) | 44.0 | 61.0 | +38.8 |
| Movement time (s) | 0.266 | 0.250 | -6.8 |
| Working path (cm) | 62.0 | 65.0 | +4.8 |
| Average speed (m/s) | 2.330 | 2.600 | +11.7 |
| Average driving force (kgf) | 5.550 | 7.430 | +33.8 |
| Power (kg.m/s) | 1.310 | 1.930 | +47.3 |

Fig 5.4, "The after-effect of prior tonic work on the height of a thrown object (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999)" (PDF p. 276 / printed p. 265, verified against the page image), plots height against "number of the movement" (0-20): the first-effort curve runs from about 42 to about 49 cm, the second-effort curve from about 50 cm to about 67-69 cm, levelling after about movement 8. The authors conclude: "Thus, the repetition of the same stimulus evokes a more pronounced reaction by the body and greater development of strength and speed" (PDF p. 276 / printed p. 265).

**Why it works** — The authors attribute it to the after-effect of the preceding tonic work; the mechanism is the one in their 3.4.2 after-effect material, not restated here.

**When to apply** — Eric's baseline (course material, Inferred): training is "weighted toward high motor-unit-recruitment core/ballistic movements (squats, cleans, jumps, throws, sprints)" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 104). Inference: this is the book's concrete upper-body example for pairing a heavy press with a light throw in one session (for example, heavy bench sets, about 10 minutes' rest, then medicine-ball chest passes), a pairing the department could trial and measure with throw distance or velocity before adopting it.

**When NOT to apply** — Several numbers do not check out. Inference, recomputed from the table: 44.0 to 61.0 cm is +38.6%, not +38.8; 0.266 to 0.250 s is -6.0%, not -6.8; speed (+11.6) and force (+33.9) are rounding. The working path divided by time reproduces the average speeds (0.62/0.266 = 2.33; 0.65/0.250 = 2.60). The power row is about one tenth of average force times average speed (12.9 and 19.3 kgf.m/s) but not in exact proportion, and the book does not say how power was derived or what its unit scaling is; do not compute power that way from this table. The table is credited to Verkhoshansky (1977) and the figure to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999); the figure's second-effort heights reach about 67-69 cm while the table gives 61.0, and the book does not say whether the table is a mean or a different trial. Subjects, n, the thrown load and the throwing apparatus are not given. Inference: "repetition of the same stimulus" does not describe a press-then-throw design; the conclusion reads as a general after-effect statement rather than one drawn from this table. The book itself records a Western finding where shot-put performance deteriorated after preliminary throws with a heavier shot (Bischke & Morehouse 1950); see [[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]].

**Example** — The authors' own case: after 3 x 3 barbell presses at 80% of 1RM and 10 minutes' rest, the throw height rose from 44.0 to 61.0 cm in Table 5.3 (PDF p. 276-277 / printed p. 265-266).

# Post-Tetanic Potentiation (the Book's "After-Effect"): Optimal Load, Timing Window, and Sequencing Rules

**Terminology note:** the book's own term is the "after-effect"; it says that "in
physiology" this form of facilitation is called post-tetanic potentiation (printed 164).
This entry uses the book's terms.

**What it is** — When a muscle is stimulated by a series of impulses, its subsequent
activity is measurably altered, a phenomenon that, "in physiology," is called post-tetanic
potentiation, produced by a preceding maximal/near-tetanic stimulus. The Russian-literature
findings the text emphasizes: **sequencing matters**: preliminary isometric tension
followed by dynamic work improves the dynamic work (up to 20% effectiveness increase
despite fatigue), but with the *reverse* sequence (dynamic then isometric), "results
deteriorate" (printed 164). The after-effect "occurs immediately after preliminary
isometric tension. The first dynamic contraction still retains some trace of inhibitory
influence, but by the second contraction, strength increases sharply compared with its
initial level" (printed 164). **Optimal load** (moderately-qualified athletes): the largest
post-isometric dynamic-strength boost (90%, as printed; this sits beside 6.7% and 5.8% for
the other two loads tested and is a probable misprint, though recorded here as given) came
after a 50% 1RM stimulus; 25% 1RM produced only a 6.7% boost and 100% 1RM only 5.8%: "the
optimal and not the maximal load is necessary for obtaining the greatest post-work
improvement," though with rising fitness, larger loads (up to 100% max) can start producing
the post-work improvement too (Ilin, 1961). **Timing window** depends on the conditioning
stimulus: after tonic barbell-squat work, explosive isometric force rose 25% within the
first minute and continued rising to 65% after 4-5 minutes (time-to-peak-force also dropped
2.6% immediately, 4.6% after 3-4 minutes); for vertical jump specifically, barbell squats
potentiated jump height by 6.8% at 3-4 minutes post, while depth jumps potentiated jump
height by 8.0% but peaked later, at 8-10 minutes post. In a separate Ilin (1961) dataset on
preliminary isometric tension, "the maximum was achieved most rapidly with loads of 25% of
1RM (after 12 minutes), and most slowly with 100% of 1RM (after 15.4 minutes) and 50% of
1RM (after 17.2 minutes)," quoted as printed (printed 165): note the numbers themselves make
50% the slowest of the three to peak, not 100%, so the load-to-timing relationship is not
perfectly monotonic across every study cited, and this entry does not try to smooth that
over. The text also cautions that "over-excitation of the CNS has a negative effect on the
precision and coordination of movements," i.e. on athletic skill (printed 164). **Rest
interval**: optimal weightlifting inter-set rest during
the after-effect window is 2-5 minutes, increasing with the lifter's bodymass; weightlifters
who carefully time rest intervals make 20% fewer failed lifts than those who do not
(Klimonov, 1965). **Delayed effects**: moderate-volume barbell work produces a positive
tonic effect the next day or two; depth (plyometric) jumps delay their facilitative effect
by 5-6 days. (PDF pp. 175-177, printed pp. 164-166, "3.4.2 The After-Effect of Muscle
Activity," Figs 3.27-3.29.)

**Why it works** — The text frames this as a nervous-system "after-effect" or "trace"
phenomenon: any stimulus, momentary or not, leaves a lingering trace in the nervous system
reflecting its relative inertness, which is proposed as foundational to how fitness
continues rising despite periodic breaks in training. The text also separately states that
heavy dynamic work "elicits a positive after-effect in the central nervous system (CNS),
which produces a general toning influence on the motor apparatus." **Inference:** treating
the isometric-then-dynamic sequencing effect specifically as an instance of this same
central-trace/CNS-toning mechanism, rather than a purely local muscular effect, connects
two statements the text makes separately; the authors do not state this connection in one
sentence.

**When to apply** — Use this as a concrete, quantified starting template for complex/contrast
training design (heavy strength stimulus paired with an explosive movement): favor ~50% 1RM
isometric or heavy-tonic conditioning stimuli over maximal loads for athletes not yet highly
trained; expect the potentiation window to open within 1 minute and build over several
minutes, with the peak timing shifting later (toward 8-10 minutes) for a more demanding
stimulus like depth jumps versus barbell squats; and program the explosive/dynamic movement
*after* the conditioning stimulus, never the reverse order, per the sequencing finding.
**Inference:** for Baylor's programming, this offers a citable, historically-grounded
starting point (a squat-then-jump contrast pair with a 3-5 minute rest window) if the
department wants to formalize a PAP/complex-training protocol, to be validated against the
department's own force-plate (CMJ) data on actual athletes before being adopted as policy.

**When NOT to apply** — All quantified figures here come from single, older Russian studies
(Tatian 1964; Ilin 1961; Klimonov 1965) on specific lifts (barbell squat, isometric leg
extension) and specific populations; the load-to-timing relationship is shown as
non-monotonic in at least one dataset (25% 1RM peaking fastest, 50% slowest), so this
should not be flattened into a single simple "heavier load = later peak" rule. This
framework should be read alongside [[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]],
which documents that Western studies of the same general phenomenon found much weaker or
absent effects: the sequencing/timing rules here reflect the Russian dataset specifically,
not a universally-replicated finding.

**Example** — **Inference:** a contrast-training set of back squats at ~50-60% 1RM followed
3-4 minutes later by depth jumps is a direct, testable application of this framework's load
and timing findings for a Baylor athlete; per the sequencing finding above, the dynamic
movement should come after the conditioning stimulus, never before it. Note that the 50%
figure in the load-response data above refers to a preliminary *static* effort's load
(e.g. an isometric squat hold), not necessarily a back-squat training load; treat the
percentage as illustrative of relative intensity, not a literal back-squat prescription.
This example is not in the source.

**Related** — [[framework--warmup-mechanisms-and-task-specific-guidelines]] (the preceding
subsection on general warm-up, a related but distinct CNS-priming phenomenon);
[[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]] (the documented Western/Russian
disagreement on whether this effect reliably occurs at all); [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--acute-delayed-particular-cumulative-training-effect-taxonomy]]: the book's training-effect taxonomy, whose worked example (squat before sprint can potentiate or depress) links back to this PAP entry; [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--non-commutative-non-associative-training-order]]: the book's general rule that training order changes the effect, of which PAP sequencing is one case; [[case-study--arm-throw-height-after-barbell-press-tonic-work]] (5.2.3, the book's own after-effect case: throw height rose 38-40% after 3 x 3 barbell presses at 80% of 1RM with 10 minutes' rest); [[case-study--novice-strength-and-speed-strength-sequencing-experiments]] (5.3, novice experiments on ordering strength and speed-strength work; it cites this entry for the within-session after-effect, yet strength-first and speed-strength-first sessions showed no significant difference in novices)

# Cue Maximal Jump Height, Not Knee Angle; When the Dip Must Be Standard, Set It With Plinths Instead of Instructions

**What it is** — Two notes in the starting-acceleration program (PDF 583 / p.572, checked against the page image):
- Vertical jumps with the bar on the shoulders: "In this exercise, as in the depth jump, the athlete must be motivated to attain the maximum jump height without thinking about the knee angle at the end of 'yielding' (pliometric) phase." Footnote 26 adds the execution: bar on the back of the shoulders, feet "about hip-width apart", "Quickly squat down and jump straight up as high as you can. Stop and shake your legs (you can rack the bar if desired)", and "the previous pliometric phase must be executed in the way that assures the consecutive best jump height automatically, thanks to the athlete's correct understanding of the motor concepts involved in this exercise."
- Kettlebell squat jumps, footnote 27: consecutive vertical jumps "standing on two high parallel benches or plinths. During execution of this exercise, the kettlebell must come close to the floor in the low down position, but should not touch the floor. In this way, one can ensure a standard leg flexion angle, determined by the height of the plinths." Fig 22 shows three frames: standing on two stands with the bell between the feet, squatting with the bell near the floor between the stands, and jumping up (an up-down arrow beside the figure).

**Why it works** — His stated reason for the first: the yielding phase should organise itself "automatically" around the goal of best height, through "correct understanding of the motor concepts" (footnote 26). For the second, his stated reason is that the plinths "ensure a standard leg flexion angle" (footnote 27). Inference: the set-up means the athlete need not think about depth, and both remove joint-angle attention from the athlete during the jump; one leaves depth to the goal, the other builds it into the set-up.

**When to apply** — When coaching loaded or depth jumps, give the outcome (jump as high as possible, reach a marker) rather than a knee-angle instruction. When a fixed squat depth matters (for comparing sets, or for a weaker athlete who would sink too deep), use a physical stop such as plinths or a box under the bell. This matches the 9.2 depth-jump technique note to reach "some height, indicated by a marker" (PDF 576 / p.565; see [[heuristic--depth-jump-execution-cues-landing-gaze-breath]]).

**When NOT to apply** — He gives no study; the cue is a coaching opinion. It does not override the leg program's squat-jump instruction that thighs go "at least parallel to the floor" (PDF 578 / p.567), which is a depth instruction for a different exercise. Inference: an athlete who lands with knees collapsing inward still needs a technique correction; "don't think about the knee angle" is about depth at the end of the dip, not about knee alignment. The plinth set-up adds a fall risk with a loaded bell, which he does not discuss.

**Example** — His Fig 22: kettlebell squat jumps between two plinths, the bell stopping just short of the floor each rep so every rep reaches the same knee flexion (PDF 583 / p.572).

# Verkhoshansky's 6-Week Ball-Throwing Speed Program: Heavy (80%) Then Light (40%) Throws Against a Cable Apparatus, Sized From Maximal Effort in the Start Position

**What it is** — "Program for improvement of ball throwing speed" (PDF 586-588 / pp.575-577, read from the page images). It combines "light and heavy weight throwing using a special training apparatus" (Fig 23, two drawings: an athlete beside a tall vertical guide carrying a weight, and an athlete in the throwing position holding a ball attached by a horizontal cable to a gridded frame; the drawings do not show how the parts connect). Load setting: "measure the maximum effort that can be displayed by the player in the starting position for the ball throw. The light weight is equal 40% and the heavy one, 80% of this value. For example, if the maximum effort is 20 kg, the training weights will be equal to 8 kg and 18 kg respectively" (PDF 586 / p.575). Method: "the repeat-serial method. One series includes the heavy and the light weight with the first exercise executed with the heavy weight"; "a series of 1x4 with heavy weight and then 2x7 with light weight" is one set of 4 heavy then 2 sets of 7 light; 1-2 min between sets, series repeated "several times" with 4-6 min between; when maximal effort rises, "the training weights should be increased accordingly" (PDF 586). The schedule (PDF 587-588 / pp.576-577) runs five days a week for weeks 1-5 and four days in week 6. Heavy sets rise from 1 x 4 to 1 x 6; light work ranges from 1 x 8 to 4 x 8; series per session rise from 2 (weeks 1-3) to 3 (week 4) and 4 (week 5, days 1-2), then return to 2 (week 5 days 3-5, week 6), with several days mixing two series formats.

**Recorded as printed:** 80% of 20 kg is 16 kg, not the printed 18 kg (Inference: arithmetic or typographic error; 40% of 20 kg = 8 kg is right). Week 1 day 5 prints "1 x 4 with heavy weight and 2x3 with light weight" (PDF 587 / p.576), out of line with the 2 x 7 to 4 x 8 light sets around it (Inference: possible misprint for 2 x 8).

**Why it works** — He gives no mechanism on these pages beyond the heavy-first order. Inference: it is a heavy-light contrast series of the kind the authors classify among contrast methods in 7.1 ([[framework--contrast-methods-load-release-pneumatics-heavy-light-set]]), and loads set from effort in the throwing start position keep the resistance specific to that joint configuration. The 5.2.3 implement findings warn that too heavy an implement can harm technique ([[claim--implement-mass-for-speed-strength-keep-technique-and-size-per-athlete]]); the 80% heavy load here is a cable resistance, not a heavier ball.

**When to apply** — An off-season block for throwing athletes (the text says "players"; the sport is not named) with access to a cable or pulley that can be set from a measured isometric effort in the throwing start position. Keep heavy first in each series, set loads from a fresh maximum, and re-test. Plan around the expected loss of throwing feel ([[heuristic--warn-throwers-the-feel-of-the-ball-fades-and-allow-2-3-weeks-to-restore]]).

**When NOT to apply** — No outcome, population or throwing-speed data is given. The 18 kg example contradicts the 80% rule; use the rule, not the example. The apparatus is drawn, not specified (pulley ratio, handle, load path), so the 40%/80% loads cannot be copied to a different machine without re-measuring. Five days a week for six weeks with throwing technique degraded from week 3 (PDF 588 / p.577) does not fit an in-season period.

**Example** — Week 4, day 3: 1 x 4 heavy and 2 x 8 light, the series repeated 3 times, then 1 x 4 heavy and 3 x 8 light (PDF 587 / p.576).

**Related** — [[heuristic--warn-throwers-the-feel-of-the-ball-fades-and-allow-2-3-weeks-to-restore]]; [[framework--contrast-methods-load-release-pneumatics-heavy-light-set]]; [[claim--implement-mass-for-speed-strength-keep-technique-and-size-per-athlete]]; [[case-study--nedobyvailov-light-heavy-and-combined-loads-in-jumpers]]; [[case-study--twelve-week-leg-program-squats-then-barbell-jumps-then-depth-and-box-jumps]]

# A Throwing-Strength Block Temporarily Costs "the Feeling of the Ball": Warn the Players, Keep Technical Goals Out of It, Then Rest the Arm a Week and Allow 2-3 Weeks

**What it is** — "Important additional information about the program" after the ball-throwing program (PDF 588 / p.577, checked against the page image):
1. "It is possible that players will lose 'the feeling of the ball' (the feel of the throw) when the strength program is used (especially beginning the 3rd week). This is a natural result of the strength training. The coach must explain the cause of this phenomenon to players. He must also tell them that it is a temporary phenomenon and that the 'feeling of throwing' will come back when the program is completed."
2. "The low ability to throw the ball as a result of the strength training should be kept in mind when technical-tactical mastery is an aim of training."
3. "The weeks following the strength program play an important role in the training process. First of all, the load on the muscles of the throwing arm must be excluded during the first week. Then the power of throwing should be increased gradually. As a rule, 2-3 weeks is enough for the restoration of the feeling of throwing."

**Why it works** — He calls the loss "a natural result of the strength training" and gives no mechanism. Inference: this is the pattern the book describes as the long-term delayed training effect, where voluminous strength loading depresses speed-strength preparedness during the block and the gain appears after it ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]); 5.3.1 also reports that heavy strength volume can reduce explosiveness and technique ([[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]]).

**When to apply** — Before any concentrated strength or contrast block for throwers or other skill-speed athletes: tell athletes and sport coaches in advance that feel may drop from about week 3 and why; do not schedule technical-tactical goals that depend on throwing feel inside the block; after it, a week with no throwing-arm load, then a gradual build over 2-3 weeks. Eric's baseline: the department's game week ends "lifting and hard practice ... 72 hours before a Saturday game" (`docs/method-baseline.md` line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: a 2-3 week restoration window is far longer than an in-season week allows, so blocks like this belong off-season.

**When NOT to apply** — The timings (week 3 onset, one week off, 2-3 weeks to restore) are his rule of thumb for this program, with no data, sport or athlete numbers. They should not be transferred to a different strength program without checking. "Feeling" is subjective and he gives no way to measure it. Inference: a drop in throwing feel that persists past 2-3 weeks, or comes with pain, is a reason to look for overload or injury, not a sign to wait longer.

**Example** — His own: after the six-week heavy-light throwing program, no throwing-arm loading in week 7, then gradually rising throwing power, with feel back by about weeks 8-9 (PDF 588 / p.577; week numbers counted by this entry).

# Put Technical Training in the Delayed-Effect Window, and Keep Competition-Period Strength Work Short, Intense and Small

**What it is** — Three linked rules from 6.10:
1. **Strength first, technique in the rebound.** "high-volume strength loads are detrimental to one's current level of speed-strength fitness and, consequently, to technical preparation. To avoid this, it is advisable in training high level athletes to structure the programme so that strength work precedes and does not interfere with technical training. Technical training should take place in the presence of the delayed training effect of the concentrated volume of strength work, i.e. when there is recovery of work capacity and an increase in the level of speed-strength." Technique then "rapidly adjusts to the athlete's higher level of specialised work capacity and there is much less likelihood of reinforcing errors" from the "lowered functional state, caused by high-volume loads" (PDF p. 376 / printed p. 365, checked against the page image).
2. **Do not add volume while the effect emerges.** "The volume of training work, therefore, should not be increased during the period of emergence of the LDTE" (PDF p. 375 / printed p. 364, checked against the page image).
3. **Competition period.** "One should be especially cautious with strength loading during the competition period. At this time, intensive and short-term strength work can be used in a small volume to tone the neuromuscular system during competition preparation, as well as to maintain the achieved level of speed-strength preparedness if the length of the competition period exceeds the duration of the LDTE of strength loading" (PDF pp. 375-376 / printed pp. 364-365).

The authors also state that "the competitive action executed with maximal physical exertion represents the most specific of all the special training means," to be viewed "simultaneously as a highly intense means of strength training," so a strength programme should rise in intensity and be "combined with technique training so as to peak concurrently with the competitive act" (PDF p. 376). They give "the dominant role" in the strength-technique interaction to "special physical preparation, both in the yearly cycle and in long-term training" (same page).

**Why it works** — The authors' reasons: a strength-depressed state reinforces technical errors, while a higher work capacity lets the athlete "concentrate his effort more effectively, increase range of movement, decrease the time of execution of movements, improve his stability, improve the strength of muscular control over all movements and increase his resistance to fatigue" (PDF p. 376). For rule 2 they report that during emergence "it is relatively easy and painless for the body to change to intensive loading, but it will react negatively to extensive work," seen as "slowed or even decreased growth of speed-strength" (PDF p. 375).

**When to apply** — After a concentrated strength block, schedule the heaviest technical emphasis for the weeks when speed-strength is coming back up, and hold volume flat through that period. In a long competition period, keep a small dose of intense, brief strength work. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is 'maintain intensity, reduce volume'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: rule 3 says the same thing for the competition period. Eric's baseline: the in-season week has "lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: that sits with rule 3's "small volume" and "short-term" strength work; the authors give no day-level timing.

**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** Verkhoshansky's Addendum paper (9.1, "Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky, Translated from the Russian by Dr. Michael Yessis"; PDF 515 / p.504, checked against the page image) restates the emergence-period rule the other way round: "In the period of LDTE realization, volume concentrated loads are handled by the body relatively easily and without harm to the body, but intense loads negatively react to the work volume" (PDF 536 / p.525, checked against the page image). Its own example then agrees with Chapter 6: an "insignificant increase" in specialised strength volume "(by only a [f]ew percent)" to "maintain" the achieved level "led to a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results" (same page, checked against the page image; partly reconstructed: the left margin of PDF 536 is clipped in the scan). Inference: the Addendum sentence may be a translation slip: its own example fits Chapter 6, and the Addendum is a separate translation of Verkhoshansky's text, which makes a translation slip plausible. The book prints both. The authors give no number for "small volume" or for how long technical emphasis should wait. Inference: for skills that need daily practice (team-sport play), technique cannot simply wait for the strength block to end; the rule is written for "high level athletes" in events where the competitive action can be isolated, and they mention the conjugate system "successively introduces different modes of loading ... rather than separating them in time" (PDF p. 376), so the separation is a matter of emphasis.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own, from the Addendum (PDF 536 / p.525, checked against the page image): the text says its Figure 8 shows that "in triple jumpers," concentrated specialised strength loads in March-April were followed by a rise in speed-strength and results in May-June; raising strength volume "by only a [f]ew percent" to hold the gain then brought "a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results." The page switches from plural to singular here: the volume rise was "as believed by [t]he athlete," and "the ath[l]ete lost his chance to be selected in the qualifying competitions for a place on the national team." These quotes are partly reconstructed: the left margin of PDF 536 is clipped in the scan. Inference: an off-season strength block ending in March would hand over to technical and speed emphasis in April with strength volume held, not raised.

**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]], [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--keep-event-specific-competitive-stress-in-preparation]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]], [[principle--technical-mastery-needs-competition-intensity-practice]], [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]] (6.12.2, the same strength-then-technique question from a later passage); [[heuristic--loading-reduction-for-the-delayed-effect-must-outlast-1-2-weeks]] (6.12.2, the reduced-loading stage after large volumes must last far longer than the usual 1-2 week unload; its "no more volume" instruction is rule 2 here); From 9.1: [[case-study--triple-jumper-annual-cycle-two-strength-blocks-fig-8]] (Fig 8 read from the image: two strength blocks, X-XI and III-IV, and a July barbell rise from about 4 to 16 t)
